sections.title: A limit is a destination, not an arrival

board_events.text: A limit is a destination, not an arrival
As $x \to a$, the limit is the value $f(x)$ heads toward.
The limit depends on the neighbourhood of $a$ — never on $f(a)$ itself.
At $x = 1$ this gives $\frac{0}{0}$ — genuinely undefined.

segments.text: <curious>Here is the single most important idea in this entire chapter.</curious> A limit is a destination — the value a function is heading toward, not a place it must actually reach.
Put precisely: as x approaches a, the limit is the value that f of x heads toward as x gets closer and closer to a.
And here is the subtle heart of it — the limit depends only on the neighbourhood around a, and never on the value of the function at a itself.
Take this function: f of x equals x squared minus one, all over x minus one.
If you simply substitute x equals one, you get zero over zero. At that single point the function is genuinely undefined.
But look at the neighbours. Feed in zero point nine, then zero point nine nine — the outputs climb toward two. Come down from above with one point one, one point zero one — again they settle on two.
The algebra agrees. For every x except one, this fraction simplifies to x plus one, which slides straight to two.
So the limit as x approaches one is two — even though the function itself never exists at one. <whisper>Destination, not arrival.</whisper>
<curious>ye poore chapter ka sabse zaroori idea hai.</curious> Limit ek destination hai — wo value jiski taraf function jaa raha hota hai, na ki wo jagah jahan wo pahunchta hi hai.
Theek-theek kahein to: jaise-jaise x, a ki taraf approach karta hai, limit wo value hai jiski taraf f of x jaata hai.
Aur yahi iska sabse subtle point hai — limit sirf a ke aas-paas ke neighbourhood par depend karti hai, kabhi bhi f of a ki value par nahin.
Is function ko lijiye: f of x barabar x squared minus one, bata x minus one.
Agar aap seedhe x barabar one rakh dein, to zero over zero milta hai. Us ek point par function sach mein undefined hai.

Lekin neighbours ko dekhiye. Zero point nine daaliye, phir zero point nine nine — outputs two ki taraf chadhte jaate hain. Aur upar se one point one, one point zero one se aaiye — phir wahi two par settle ho jaate hain.
Algebra bhi yahi kehti hai. One ko chhodkar har x ke liye ye fraction simplify hokar x plus one ban jaata hai, jo seedha two ki taraf jaata hai.
To limit, jaise x approaches one, equals two — bhale hi function khud one par kabhi exist hi na kare. <whisper>Destination, arrival nahin.</whisper>

sections.title: One-sided limits and when a limit exists

board_events.text: Two friends walking to the same shop
If both friends reach the same shop, the destination is unambiguous.
These two friends are the left-hand limit and the right-hand limit.
Limit exists only when $\text{LHL} = \text{RHL}$ and both are finite.

board_events.text: $f(a)$ is irrelevant; oscillation like $\sin\frac{1}{x}$ near $0$ kills the limit.
'Approaching' is two-sided by default — one friend arriving is not enough.

segments.text: <curious>Picture a narrow lane in Chandni Chowk with one shop you both want to reach.</curious> Two friends walk toward it — one from the left end, one from the right.
If both friends end up standing at the very same shop, then the place you were heading is unambiguous — that is when the limit exists.
Those two friends have names. The one from the left is the left-hand limit, L H L. The one from the right is the right-hand limit, R H L.
The left-hand limit is where f heads as x creeps up to a from values smaller than a; the right-hand limit, from values larger than a.
And here is the rule that governs the whole chapter — the limit exists only when both friends meet: L H L equals R H L, and both are finite.

On the left, both curves converge to the same height L, so the limit exists. On the right, the lane secretly forks — the left-walker lands at one height, the right-walker at another. No single destination, so no limit.

Two warnings. First, the value f of a is completely irrelevant — it may be undefined, or defined but different. Second, a function that oscillates forever, like sine of one over x near zero, never settles, so no limit exists.
And remember, plain limit notation is two-sided by default. One friend reaching the shop is never enough; you always need both sides to agree.
<curious>Chandni Chowk ki ek tang gali sochiye, jismein ek hi shop hai jahan aap dono pahunchna chahte hain.</curious> Do dost uski taraf chalte hain — ek baayen chhor se, ek daayen chhor se.
Agar dono dost bilkul usi shop par aakar khade hon, to jagah jahan aap jaa rahe the wo saaf hai — tabhi limit exist karti hai.
In dono doston ke naam hain. Baayen wala hai left-hand limit, L H L. Daayen wala hai right-hand limit, R H L.
Left-hand limit wo hai jahan f jaata hai jab x, a se chhoti values se a tak pahunchta hai; aur right-hand limit, badi values se.
Aur yahi rule poore chapter ko chalata hai — limit tabhi exist karti hai jab dono dost milen: L H L barabar R H L, aur dono finite hon.

Baayin taraf, dono curves ek hi height L par milte hain, to limit exist karti hai. Daayin taraf gali chupke se fork ho jaati hai — baaya ek height par, daaya doosri par. Koi ek destination nahin, to limit nahin.

Do warnings. Pehla, f of a ki value bilkul irrelevant hai — wo undefined ho sakti hai ya defined par alag. Doosra, jo function hamesha oscillate karta rahe, jaise sine of one over x zero ke paas, wo kabhi settle nahin hota, to limit nahin.
Aur yaad rakhiye, plain limit by default two-sided hoti hai. Ek dost ka shop par pahunch jaana kaafi nahin; hamesha dono sides ka agree karna zaroori hai.

sections.title: When substitution fails: the 0/0 toolkit

board_events.text: When substitution fails: the 0/0 toolkit
Algebra of limits is legal because destinations simply add and multiply.
Quotient rule needs $M \neq 0$ — dividing by something vanishing explodes.
Cancel $(x-a)$, then substitute $x=a$: each of the $n$ terms becomes $a^{n-1}$.
Procedure A — factor and cancel $(x-a)$; Procedure B — multiply by the conjugate.

segments.text: Substituting is always your first move. But when it hands you zero over zero, that is not a dead end — it is an instruction to do more work.

Why are the algebra-of-limits rules even legal? Because near a, each function sits arbitrarily close to its target, so their sum sits close to the sum of targets, and their product close to the product.
The quotient rule carries one non-negotiable caveat: the denominator's limit must not be zero. Divide by something vanishingly small and the ratio explodes.
This is the star limit you will reuse everywhere. Let me show you why it is true.
Substitution gives zero over zero, so x equals a must be a root of the top. That means x minus a factors out cleanly, leaving this sum of n terms.
Cancel the common x minus a — legal, because for the limit x is never exactly a. Now substitute x equals a. There are exactly n terms, and each becomes a to the n minus one.
So your two workhorses. For a rational zero over zero, factor out x minus a from top and bottom and cancel. For a surd, multiply and divide by the conjugate to clear the root.
The conjugate trick rests on this identity — root p minus root q, times root p plus root q, equals p minus q. That kills the square root and exposes a cancellable x minus a.
Substitute karna hamesha pehla kadam hai. Lekin jab wo zero over zero de de, to wo dead end nahin hai — wo ek instruction hai ki aur kaam karo.

Algebra-of-limits ke rules aakhir allowed kyun hain? Kyunki a ke paas har function apne target ke behad kareeb hota hai, to unka sum, targets ke sum ke kareeb, aur product, products ke kareeb baithta hai.
Quotient rule ki ek shart kabhi nahin tootti: denominator ki limit zero nahin honi chahiye. Kisi bahut chhoti cheez se divide karo aur ratio phat padta hai.
Ye hai wo star limit jise aap har jagah reuse karenge. Chaliye dikhata hoon ye sach kyun hai.
Substitution zero over zero deta hai, to x equals a upar wale ka ek root hona chahiye. Matlab x minus a saaf-saaf factor ho jaata hai, aur peeche ye n terms ka sum bachta hai.
Common x minus a ko cancel kijiye — ye legal hai, kyunki limit ke liye x kabhi exactly a hota hi nahin. Ab x equals a rakhiye. Theek n terms hain, aur har ek banta hai a to the n minus one.
To aapke do workhorses. Rational zero over zero ke liye, upar-neeche se x minus a factor karke cancel kijiye. Surd ke liye, conjugate se multiply aur divide karke root hataiye.
Conjugate trick isi identity par tiki hai — root p minus root q, into root p plus root q, barabar p minus q. Ye square root ko khatm karke ek cancel hone layak x minus a saamne le aati hai.

sections.title: The existence test and the algebra of limits

board_events.text: Your limits toolkit — the core rules

board_events.latex: \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) = L
\lim(f \pm g) = L \pm M, \quad \lim(kf) = kL, \quad \lim(f \cdot g) = L \cdot M

board_events.text: $\frac{0}{0},\ \frac{\infty}{\infty},\ \infty-\infty,\ 0\times\infty$ are indeterminate — resolve, never guess.

segments.text: Here is your complete algebra toolkit for limits, all in one place for quick recall.
The existence test: the limit equals L exactly when the left-hand and right-hand limits both equal L and are finite.
In practice you compute the two sides with a small positive h — f of a minus h for the left, f of a plus h for the right.
Sums, differences, scalar multiples, and products all split freely into the limits L and M.
The quotient splits too, but only when M is not zero. Powers pass straight through to L to the n.
For polynomials and for rationals with a non-zero denominator, direct substitution simply works — plug in a and read the answer.
And the star algebraic limit, valid for all rational n — memorise this one; it powers half the chapter.
Finally, the indeterminate forms — zero over zero, infinity over infinity, infinity minus infinity, zero times infinity. None of these is an answer. Each is a signal to resolve by algebra.
Yahan hai aapki poori limits ki algebra toolkit, ek hi jagah quick recall ke liye.
Existence test: limit barabar L tabhi hai jab left-hand aur right-hand limit dono barabar L hon aur finite hon.
Practice mein aap dono sides ko ek small positive h se nikalte hain — left ke liye f of a minus h, right ke liye f of a plus h.
Sums, differences, scalar multiples, aur products sab aaraam se limits L aur M mein bant jaate hain.
Quotient bhi banta hai, par sirf tab jab M zero na ho. Powers seedhe L to the n tak pass ho jaate hain.
Polynomials ke liye aur un rationals ke liye jinka denominator zero na ho, direct substitution bas kaam kar jaata hai — a rakhiye aur answer padhiye.
Aur wo star algebraic limit, har rational n ke liye valid — ise yaad kar lijiye; ye aadhe chapter ko chalati hai.
Aakhir mein, indeterminate forms — zero over zero, infinity over infinity, infinity minus infinity, zero times infinity. Inmein se koi answer nahin hai. Har ek algebra se resolve karne ka signal hai.

sections.title: Factoring a 0/0 limit, and the ratio trick

board_events.text: Worked example: a clean 0/0 by factoring
Step 1 — substitute $x=3$: top $= 0$, bottom $= 0$. Form is $\frac{0}{0}$.
Always declare the $\frac{0}{0}$ form before factoring — boards award method marks for it.
Speed trap: do not factor a degree-18 polynomial

segments.text: Let us evaluate the limit, as x approaches three, of x squared minus two x minus three, over x minus three.
Step one, always substitute first. At x equals three the top is nine minus six minus three, which is zero, and the bottom is zero too. So the form is zero over zero — resolve.
Step two, factor the numerator. x squared minus two x minus three factors neatly into x minus three, times x plus one.
The x minus three cancels top and bottom, leaving x plus one. Substitute three: three plus one is four. That is our limit.
A presentation habit worth marks: always write down that the form is zero over zero before you factor. Boards reward you just for spotting it.
<curious>Now a genuine speed trap.</curious> Evaluate the limit as x approaches one of x to the eighteen minus one, over x to the twelve minus one.
A panicking student tries to factor degree eighteen. Do not. Both pieces have the shape x to the n minus one, so divide top and bottom by x minus one and use the star limit on each.

The top gives eighteen, the bottom gives twelve, so the answer is eighteen over twelve, which is three over two. <whisper>The shortcut: for x to the m minus one over x to the n minus one at one, the answer is just m over n.</whisper>
Chaliye evaluate karte hain limit, jaise x approaches three, of x squared minus two x minus three, bata x minus three.
Step one, hamesha pehle substitute kijiye. X equals three par top hai nine minus six minus three, yaani zero, aur bottom bhi zero. To form hai zero over zero — resolve kijiye.
Step two, numerator ko factor kijiye. X squared minus two x minus three saaf-saaf banta hai x minus three, into x plus one.
X minus three upar-neeche cancel ho jaata hai, bachta hai x plus one. Three rakhiye: three plus one barabar four. Yahi hamari limit hai.
Ek presentation aadat jo marks dilati hai: factor karne se pehle hamesha likhiye ki form zero over zero hai. Boards ise pehchanne ke marks dete hain.
<curious>Ab ek asli speed trap.</curious> Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x approaches one, of x to the eighteen minus one, bata x to the twelve minus one.

Ghabraya hua student degree eighteen ko factor karne lagta hai. Mat kijiye. Dono pieces ka shape hai x to the n minus one, to top aur bottom ko x minus one se divide kijiye aur har ek par star limit lagaiye.

Top deta hai eighteen, bottom deta hai twelve, to answer hai eighteen over twelve, yaani three over two. <whisper>Shortcut: x to the m minus one over x to the n minus one, one par, answer bas m over n hota hai.</whisper>

sections.title: Fractional powers, and the find-a-b problem

board_events.text: Worked example: the star limit with fractional powers
Both pieces vanish at $x=1$ ($\frac{0}{0}$). Insert $(x-1)$ into each.
Advanced: find a and b so the limit is finite
Denominator $\to 0$, so for a finite limit the numerator must also $\to 0$.

segments.text: Evaluate the limit as x approaches one of x to the one-third minus one, over x to the one-half minus one.
Both top and bottom vanish at x equals one, giving zero over zero. The trick is to insert an x minus one underneath each piece.
Now each piece is exactly the star limit with a equals one, so the top tends to one-third and the bottom to one-half.
One-third divided by one-half is one-third times two, which is two over three. That is the limit.
Now a favourite advanced problem. Find a and b so that the limit as x approaches two of x squared plus a x plus b, over x squared minus x minus two, equals five over three.
Here is the whole game. The denominator factors to x minus two, times x plus one, so it vanishes at two. For the overall limit to stay finite, the numerator is forced to vanish at two as well.
Setting the numerator to zero at x equals two gives four plus two a plus b equals zero, that is two a plus b equals minus four. One condition down.

Since x minus two divides the top, write it as x minus two, times x minus c. The limit becomes two minus c over three, set equal to five over three, giving c equals minus three. So the numerator is x minus two times x plus three, meaning a is one and b is minus six.
Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x approaches one, of x to the one-third minus one, bata x to the one-half minus one.
Top aur bottom dono x equals one par vanish ho jaate hain, zero over zero dekar. Trick hai har piece ke neeche ek x minus one daal dena.
Ab har piece bilkul star limit hai, a equals one ke saath, to top jaata hai one-third ki taraf aur bottom one-half ki taraf.
One-third divided by one-half barabar one-third into two, yaani two over three. Yahi limit hai.
Ab ek favourite advanced problem. A aur b aise dhoondhiye ki limit, jaise x approaches two, of x squared plus a x plus b, bata x squared minus x minus two, barabar five over three ho.

Yahi poora khel hai. Denominator factor hokar banta hai x minus two, into x plus one, to two par vanish ho jaata hai. Overall limit finite rahe iske liye numerator ko bhi two par vanish hona hi padega.
Numerator ko x equals two par zero rakhne se milta hai four plus two a plus b barabar zero, yaani two a plus b barabar minus four. Ek condition ho gayi.

Kyunki x minus two, top ko divide karta hai, ise likhiye x minus two, into x minus c. Limit banti hai two minus c over three, ise five over three ke barabar rakhiye, to c barabar minus three. To numerator hai x minus two into x plus three, yaani a barabar one aur b barabar minus six.

sections.title: Traps: limit vs value, 0/0, quotient rule, the m/n shortcut

board_events.text: The four traps that cost marks
Trap 1: confusing $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ with $f(a)$.
Trap 2: treating $\frac{0}{0}$ as a final answer.
Trap 3: applying the quotient rule when the denominator's limit is $0$.
Pro-tip: substitute first. A clean number means one line, done.
See a vanishing denominator with a finite limit? Write 'numerator must $\to 0$.'

segments.text: Let us lock in the four mistakes that quietly cost the most marks in this subtopic.

Trap one, the single most common conceptual error — confusing the limit with the function value. The limit is the destination; the value is whether you arrive. They often differ, and the limit does not care about f of a at all.
Trap two, treating zero over zero as if it were an answer. It is neither zero nor 'does not exist' — it is an instruction to factor or rationalise.
Trap three, firing the quotient rule when the denominator's limit is zero. The rule demands M not equal to zero — skip that check and you will prove nonsense.
Trap four, misfiring the m over n shortcut. It holds only as x approaches one. Around any other point, fall back to the full n a to the n minus one ratio.
<whisper>The pro reflex — always substitute first.</whisper> A clean number means you are finished in one line; only the indeterminate cases earn the heavy machinery.
And one reflex cracks almost every find-a-b problem — the instant you see a finite limit with a vanishing denominator, immediately write 'the numerator must also head to zero.'
Chaliye un chaar galtiyon ko pakka kar lein jo is subtopic mein chupchaap sabse zyada marks kha jaati hain.

Trap one, sabse common conceptual galti — limit ko function value se confuse karna. Limit destination hai; value ye ki aap pahunche ya nahin. Ye aksar alag hote hain, aur limit ko f of a ki parwaah hi nahin.
Trap two, zero over zero ko answer maan lena. Ye na zero hai na 'does not exist' — ye factor ya rationalise karne ka instruction hai.
Trap three, quotient rule chala dena jab denominator ki limit zero ho. Rule maangta hai M zero ke barabar na ho — ye check chhodiye aur aap bakwaas prove kar baithenge.
Trap four, m over n shortcut ko galat jagah chala dena. Ye sirf x approaches one par kaam karti hai. Kisi aur point par, poore n a to the n minus one ratio par wapas aaiye.
<whisper>Pro reflex — hamesha pehle substitute kijiye.</whisper> Clean number mila to aap ek line mein done; sirf indeterminate cases hi heavy machinery ke layak hain.
Aur ek reflex lagbhag har find-a-b problem ko khol deta hai — jaise hi finite limit ke saath vanishing denominator dikhe, turant likhiye 'numerator ko bhi zero ki taraf jaana hi hoga.'

sections.title: A 0/0 you cannot factor

board_events.text: A 0/0 you cannot factor
$\sin x$ is not a polynomial — the factoring toolkit fails completely.
So we prove a few stubborn limits once, then memorise and reuse them.
These pre-proven results are the standard limits — the junctions of calculus.

board_events.caption: Near the origin, y = sin x and y = x are twins

segments.text: <curious>Meet a new kind of troublemaker.</curious> The limit as x approaches zero of sine x over x. Substitute and you get zero over zero, just like before — but now there is nothing to factor.
Sine x is not a polynomial. You cannot pull a clean x out of it by algebra. The entire factoring toolkit fails here.
So mathematicians did the sensible thing — they proved a handful of these stubborn limits once, rigorously, and everyone agrees to memorise and reuse them, exactly like multiplication tables.

Think of the Indian Railways network. To cross the country you route through a major junction. Standard limits are exactly those junctions — reshape any messy limit until it passes through a known one, read off the value, and continue.
Here is the flagship junction — sine x over x tends to one as x tends to zero.

Why should this be one? Zoom right into the graph near the origin. The curve y equals sine x becomes indistinguishable from the straight line y equals x. For tiny angles they are twins, so their ratio heads to one.
The same twins-near-zero idea powers the exponential and logarithmic junctions. For small x, e to the x is about one plus x, and log of one plus x is about x.
So e to the x minus one over x tends to one, and log of one plus x over x tends to one. These two, with the sine result, are the most reused limit facts in all of calculus.

<curious>Ek nayi tarah ke troublemaker se miliye.</curious> Limit, jaise x approaches zero, of sine x over x. Substitute kijiye to zero over zero milta hai, pehle jaisa hi — par ab factor karne ko kuch hai hi nahin.
Sine x ek polynomial nahin hai. Aap algebra se ismein se ek saaf x nahin kheench sakte. Poori factoring toolkit yahan fail ho jaati hai.
To mathematicians ne samajhdaari ka kaam kiya — in kuch ziddi limits ko ek baar, rigorously prove kar diya, aur sab inhein memorise karke reuse karte hain, bilkul multiplication tables ki tarah.

Indian Railways ke network ko sochiye. Desh paar karne ke liye aap kisi bade junction se route karte hain. Standard limits bilkul wahi junctions hain — kisi bhi messy limit ko reshape kijiye jab tak wo kisi known junction se na guzre, value padhiye, aur aage badhiye.
Ye raha flagship junction — sine x over x jaata hai one ki taraf, jaise x jaata hai zero ki taraf.

Ye one kyun hona chahiye? Origin ke paas graph mein zoom kijiye. Curve y equals sine x, seedhi line y equals x se indistinguishable ho jaata hai. Bahut chhote angles ke liye ye twins hain, to inka ratio one ki taraf jaata hai.
Yahi twins-near-zero idea exponential aur logarithmic junctions ko chalata hai. Chhote x ke liye, e to the x lagbhag one plus x hai, aur log of one plus x lagbhag x.

To e to the x minus one over x jaata hai one ki taraf, aur log of one plus x over x jaata hai one ki taraf. Ye do, sine wale result ke saath, poore calculus mein sabse zyada reuse hone wale limit facts hain.

sections.title: Four conditions: break one, lose the marks

board_events.text: Four conditions — break one, lose the marks
Radians only. In degrees, $\frac{\sin x}{x} \to \frac{\pi}{180}$.
Condition 2 — the argument must actually go to $0$.
Mismatch the boxes and you mismatch the answer.
Note the power before you quote a value.

segments.text: These junctions are powerful, but they come with four conditions. Break any one and the answer changes.
Condition one, radians only. Sine x over x tends to one only when x is in radians. In degrees the answer is pi over one hundred eighty, not one.
Condition two, the argument must genuinely go to zero. Sine x over x at x approaching pi is just zero over pi, which is zero. The magic only happens when the angle itself shrinks to zero.
Condition three, the arguments must match. The real result is sine of a box, over the same box, tends to one. So sine five x over five x is one, but sine five x over x is five.
So if you mismatch the boxes, you mismatch the answer. This is the most common silent error in the whole subtopic — always match top and bottom.
Condition four, the denominator power matters. One minus cosine x over x tends to zero, but one minus cosine x over x squared tends to one-half. Same numerator, completely different destinations.
So always note the power before you quote a value. A single wrong exponent silently flips a correct method into a wrong answer.
Ye junctions powerful hain, par inke saath chaar conditions hain. Kisi ek ko todiye aur answer badal jaata hai.
Condition one, sirf radians. Sine x over x, one ki taraf tabhi jaata hai jab x radians mein ho. Degrees mein answer hai pi over one hundred eighty, one nahin.
Condition two, argument ko sach mein zero ki taraf jaana chahiye. Sine x over x, x approaching pi par bas zero over pi hai, yaani zero. Jaadu tabhi hota hai jab angle khud zero tak simte.
Condition three, arguments ka match hona zaroori hai. Asli result hai sine of a box, over the same box, jaata hai one ki taraf. To sine five x over five x hai one, par sine five x over x hai five.
To agar boxes mismatch hue, to answer bhi mismatch. Ye is poore subtopic ki sabse common silent galti hai — top aur bottom hamesha match kijiye.

Condition four, denominator ki power maayne rakhti hai. One minus cosine x over x jaata hai zero ki taraf, par one minus cosine x over x squared jaata hai one-half ki taraf. Ek hi numerator, bilkul alag destinations.
To value batane se pehle hamesha power note kijiye. Ek galat exponent chupchaap ek sahi method ko galat answer mein badal deta hai.

sections.title: The engine: the Squeeze Theorem and the geometric proof

board_events.text: The engine: the Sandwich (Squeeze) Theorem
If $g \le f \le h$ near $a$ and $g, h \to L$, then $f \to L$ too.

board_events.text: As $x \to 0$, $\cos x \to 1$, so the ratio is squeezed to $1$.
The $e$ junction comes from the series $e^{x} = 1 + x + \frac{x^{2}}{2!} + \cdots$

segments.text: Where does sine x over x equals one actually come from? From the Sandwich, or Squeeze, Theorem.

The idea is simple. If f is trapped between g and h near a, and both g and h head to the same limit L, then f has nowhere to go but L. A function squeezed between two slices of bread that meet must go to the meeting point.
Take a unit circle and a small angle x. Three regions nest inside one another — triangle O A P sits inside the sector O A P, which sits inside the larger triangle O A T.

Comparing their areas gives half sine x, less than half x, less than half tangent x. That middle area is half x only because x is in radians — this is the exact spot where radian measure is essential.
Multiply through by two and divide by sine x. Rearranged, this says cosine x is less than sine x over x, which is less than one.
As x heads to zero, cosine x heads to one. The ratio is sandwiched between something tending to one and one itself — so by the Squeeze Theorem, sine x over x tends to one.
The one minus cosine junction follows quickly. Using one minus cosine x equals two sine squared x over two, the whole thing becomes one-half times a sine-over-angle squared, which tends to one-half.

And the exponential junction comes from the series for e to the x. Since e to the x minus one equals x times one plus x over two factorial and onward, dividing by x leaves one plus small terms — which tends to one.
Sine x over x barabar one aakhir aata kahan se hai? Sandwich, ya Squeeze, Theorem se.

Idea simple hai. Agar f, a ke paas g aur h ke beech phansa hai, aur g aur h dono ek hi limit L ki taraf jaate hain, to f ke paas L ke siwa kahin jaane ki jagah nahin. Bread ke do slices ke beech dabaa function usi milan-bindu par jaata hai.
Ek unit circle aur ek chhota angle x lijiye. Teen regions ek-doosre ke andar baithte hain — triangle O A P, sector O A P ke andar, jo bade triangle O A T ke andar.

Inke areas ki tulna deti hai half sine x, less than half x, less than half tangent x. Wo beech wala area half x sirf isliye hai kyunki x radians mein hai — yahi wo jagah hai jahan radian measure zaroori hai.
Poore ko two se multiply kijiye aur sine x se divide kijiye. Rearrange karne par ye kehta hai cosine x, sine x over x se kam, jo one se kam.
Jaise x zero ki taraf jaata hai, cosine x one ki taraf jaata hai. Ratio ek one ki taraf jaati cheez aur khud one ke beech dabi hai — to Squeeze Theorem se, sine x over x jaata hai one ki taraf.

One minus cosine junction jhat se nikal aata hai. One minus cosine x barabar two sine squared x over two istemaal karke, poori cheez banti hai one-half into sine-over-angle ka square, jo one-half ki taraf jaata hai.

Aur exponential junction, e to the x ki series se aata hai. Kyunki e to the x minus one barabar x into one plus x over two factorial waghairah, x se divide karne par bachta hai one plus chhote terms — jo one ki taraf jaata hai.

sections.title: The standard-limit junction table

board_events.text: The standard-limit junction table
Every argument is in radians and tends to $0$ — no exceptions.

segments.text: Here is the full junction table — commit every line to memory. All arguments are in radians and tend to zero.
The trigonometric junctions — sine x, tangent x, inverse sine x, and inverse tangent x, each over x, all tend to one.
The half-angle junction — one minus cosine x over x squared tends to one-half. With a k inside, it becomes k squared over two — remember to square the k.
The exponential and logarithmic junctions — e to the x minus one over x tends to one, a to the x minus one over x tends to log a, and log of one plus x over x tends to one.
The two definitions of the number e — one plus x to the one over x tends to e, and one plus one over n, all to the n, tends to e as n grows.
And the one-to-the-infinity rule — when f tends to one and g tends to infinity, the whole power equals e raised to the limit of g times f minus one.
And the argument-matching generalisation for a constant k — sine of k x over x tends to k, and e to the k x minus one over x tends to k.
One reminder stamped over the whole table — every single argument is in radians and tends to zero. There are no exceptions.
Ye rahi poori junction table — har line memorise kar lijiye. Saare arguments radians mein hain aur zero ki taraf jaate hain.
Trigonometric junctions — sine x, tangent x, inverse sine x, aur inverse tangent x, har ek over x, sab one ki taraf jaate hain.
Half-angle junction — one minus cosine x over x squared jaata hai one-half ki taraf. Andar k ho, to ye banta hai k squared over two — k ko square karna yaad rakhiye.
Exponential aur logarithmic junctions — e to the x minus one over x jaata hai one, a to the x minus one over x jaata hai log a, aur log of one plus x over x jaata hai one.
Number e ki do definitions — one plus x to the one over x jaata hai e, aur one plus one over n, all to the n, jaata hai e jaise n badhta hai.
Aur one-to-the-infinity rule — jab f jaata hai one ki taraf aur g jaata hai infinity ki taraf, to poora power barabar e raised to the limit of g into f minus one.
Aur constant k ke liye argument-matching generalisation — sine of k x over x jaata hai k, aur e to the k x minus one over x jaata hai k.
Poori table par ek reminder — har ek argument radians mein hai aur zero ki taraf jaata hai. Koi exception nahin.

sections.title: Routing pieces through junctions, and squaring the k

board_events.text: Worked example: route both pieces through junctions
Speed trap: square the k
Argument is $4x$, not $x$ — use $\frac{k^{2}}{2}$, not $\frac{1}{2}$.
Mixing an exponential and a trig junction

segments.text: Evaluate the limit as x approaches zero of sine five x over sine three x.

The plan is to reshape both pieces into the canonical sine of a box over the box form. Insert the matching arguments — five x under the top sine, three x under the bottom sine — and carry the leftover five x over three x.
The first factor tends to one, the second tends to one, and the third is just the constant five over three. So the answer is five over three.
<curious>Now a fast speed trap.</curious> Evaluate the limit as x approaches zero of one minus cosine four x over x squared.
The trap: students blindly answer one-half, forgetting the argument is four x, not x. The correct generalised junction is one minus cosine of k x over x squared tends to k squared over two.
So with k equal to four, the answer is four squared over two, which is sixteen over two, which is eight. Square the k — that is the whole mental shortcut.
Evaluate the limit as x approaches zero of e to the two x minus one, over sine three x — this mixes two junction types.

Route the top through the e junction with two x, and the bottom through the sine junction with three x. Both bracketed pieces tend to one, leaving the constant two over three. So the limit is two over three.
Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x approaches zero, of sine five x over sine three x.

Plan hai dono pieces ko canonical sine of a box over the box shape mein laana. Matching arguments daaliye — top sine ke neeche five x, bottom sine ke neeche three x — aur bacha hua five x over three x saath le chaliye.
Pehla factor jaata hai one, doosra jaata hai one, aur teesra bas constant five over three hai. To answer hai five over three.
<curious>Ab ek tez speed trap.</curious> Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x approaches zero, of one minus cosine four x over x squared.
Trap: students aankh moondkar one-half likh dete hain, ye bhoolkar ki argument four x hai, x nahin. Sahi generalised junction hai one minus cosine of k x over x squared jaata hai k squared over two.
To k barabar four ke saath, answer hai four squared over two, yaani sixteen over two, yaani eight. K ko square kijiye — yahi poora mental shortcut hai.
Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x approaches zero, of e to the two x minus one, bata sine three x — ye do junction types ko mix karta hai.

Top ko e junction se two x ke saath route kijiye, aur bottom ko sine junction se three x ke saath. Dono bracketed pieces one ki taraf jaate hain, bachta hai constant two over three. To limit hai two over three.

sections.title: Taming a 1-to-the-infinity form

board_events.text: Advanced: taming a 1-to-the-infinity form
As $x \to 0$, $\cos x \to 1$ and $\frac{1}{x^{2}} \to \infty$ — the form is $1^{\infty}$.
The pattern to internalise
Spot a base $\to 1$ with an exponent $\to \infty$? Write $e^{\lim g(f-1)}$ at once.

segments.text: Evaluate the limit as x approaches zero of cosine x, raised to the power one over x squared.
Identify the form first. As x heads to zero, cosine x heads to one and one over x squared heads to infinity. This is the indeterminate form one to the infinity.
Reach straight for the rule — the limit equals e raised to the limit of g times f minus one, with f equal to cosine x and g equal to one over x squared.
So compute g times f minus one — that is cosine x minus one over x squared. Flip the sign to recognise our familiar junction: it is minus one minus cosine x over x squared, which is minus one-half.
Therefore the whole expression tends to e to the minus one-half, which is one over root e. <whisper>The rule turned a frightening exponent into a familiar cosine junction in one move.</whisper>
Notice the pattern across all four of these. Every problem is made to pass through a junction — you multiply and divide until each piece is canonical, collect the leftover constant, and read off.

And the instant you spot a base tending to one with an exponent tending to infinity, do not panic — write e to the limit of g times f minus one immediately, and the one-to-the-infinity monster becomes an ordinary limit.
Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x approaches zero, of cosine x, raised to the power one over x squared.
Pehle form pehchaniye. Jaise x zero ki taraf jaata hai, cosine x one ki taraf aur one over x squared infinity ki taraf. Ye indeterminate form hai one to the infinity.
Seedhe rule uthaiye — limit barabar e raised to the limit of g into f minus one, jahan f barabar cosine x aur g barabar one over x squared.

To nikaliye g into f minus one — yaani cosine x minus one over x squared. Sign paltiye taaki hamara jaana-pehchana junction dikhe: ye hai minus, one minus cosine x over x squared, yaani minus one-half.

Isliye poori expression jaati hai e to the minus one-half ki taraf, yaani one over root e. <whisper>Rule ne ek daraawne exponent ko ek hi move mein jaane-pehchane cosine junction mein badal diya.</whisper>

In chaaron mein pattern dekhiye. Har problem ko kisi junction se guzaara jaata hai — aap multiply aur divide karte hain jab tak har piece canonical na ho, bacha hua constant ikattha karte hain, aur answer padh lete hain.

Aur jaise hi base one ki taraf aur exponent infinity ki taraf dikhe, ghabraiye mat — turant likhiye e to the limit of g into f minus one, aur one-to-the-infinity ka monster ek ordinary limit ban jaata hai.

sections.title: Traps: degrees, argument mismatch, cos power, base confusion

board_events.text: The four standard-limit traps
Trap 1: degrees instead of radians ($\to \frac{\pi}{180}$).
Trap 2: argument mismatch ($\frac{\sin kx}{x} = k$).
Trap 3: wrong denominator power for $1 - \cos$ (remember to square the $k$).
Pro-tip: force every piece through a junction, collect the constant.
See a power $\to \infty$ with base $\to 1$? Write $e^{\lim g(f-1)}$ instantly.

segments.text: Four traps guard this subtopic. Each one silently converts a correct method into a wrong number.
Trap one, degrees instead of radians. Sine x over x equals one holds only in radians; a stray degree symbol changes the answer to pi over one hundred eighty. Always check the angle's units first.
Trap two, argument mismatch. Sine of k x over x is k, not one. The standard limit needs the same expression inside the function and on the bottom — match the boxes.
Trap three, the wrong denominator power for one minus cosine. Over x it tends to zero, over x squared it tends to one-half, and with a k inside remember to square the k.
Trap four, base confusion. e to the x minus one over x tends to one, but a to the x minus one over x tends to log a. Only base e gives a clean one.

<whisper>The pro habit — make every problem pass through a junction.</whisper> Multiply and divide to force each trig, exp, or log piece into its canonical shape, collect the leftover constants, and read off the answer.

And the instant you see a power tending to infinity with a base tending to one, write e to the limit of g times f minus one immediately — you have turned a one-to-the-infinity monster into an ordinary limit.
Chaar traps is subtopic ki rakhwaali karte hain. Har ek chupchaap ek sahi method ko galat number mein badal deta hai.

Trap one, radians ki jagah degrees. Sine x over x barabar one sirf radians mein sahi hai; ek bhatka hua degree symbol answer ko pi over one hundred eighty bana deta hai. Pehle hamesha angle ki units check kijiye.
Trap two, argument mismatch. Sine of k x over x hai k, one nahin. Standard limit ko function ke andar aur bottom par ek hi expression chahiye — boxes match kijiye.
Trap three, one minus cosine ke liye galat denominator power. Over x wo jaata hai zero, over x squared wo jaata hai one-half, aur andar k ho to k ko square karna yaad rakhiye.
Trap four, base confusion. e to the x minus one over x jaata hai one, par a to the x minus one over x jaata hai log a. Sirf base e ek clean one deta hai.

<whisper>Pro aadat — har problem ko junction se guzaariye.</whisper> Multiply aur divide karke har trig, exp, ya log piece ko uske canonical shape mein laiye, bache hue constants ikattha kijiye, aur answer padhiye.
Aur jaise hi power infinity ki taraf aur base one ki taraf dikhe, turant likhiye e to the limit of g into f minus one — aapne one-to-the-infinity monster ko ordinary limit bana diya.

board_events.text: How fast are you going right now?
The speedometer measures distance over a tiny sliver of time, then shrinks the sliver.
As the interval shrinks to zero, the average settles on the instantaneous rate.

board_events.text: The numerator is the change in output; $h$ is the shrinking sliver of input.
The whole thing is a $\frac{0}{0}$ limit — all your limit machinery powers derivatives.
Evaluate at every point and $f'(x)$ becomes a brand-new function.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a genuinely deep question — how fast is your car going at this exact instant?</curious> Average speed is easy: distance over time. But 'right now' is a single instant, and in an instant no time passes.

So it looks like we would compute change over zero — nonsense. Yet your speedometer answers confidently. Its trick: measure distance over a tiny sliver of time and divide, then make the sliver smaller and smaller.
As the time-window shrinks toward zero, that average-over-a-sliver settles onto a single definite number — your instantaneous speed. That limiting process is exactly the derivative.

The same idea is purely geometric. Join two points on a curve by a secant line — its slope is the average rate between them. Now slide the second point toward the first: the secant pivots until it becomes the tangent that just grazes the curve.
Formalising both pictures gives the first principle, also called the ab-initio or delta method. The derivative f dash of x is the limit, as h goes to zero, of f of x plus h minus f of x, all over h.

Read it piece by piece: the numerator is the change in output; the h in the denominator is the shrinking sliver of input. Slope of tangent and instantaneous rate are the two faces of this one expression.
And notice what it really is — a zero over zero limit. Everything you learned about limits and standard limits is precisely the machinery that makes derivatives work.
One more thing. f dash at a single point a is a number — one slope. But evaluate the derivative at every point and you get a brand-new function, f dash of x.

<curious>Ek sach mein gehra sawaal — abhi is exact instant par aapki car kitni tez chal rahi hai?</curious> Average speed aasaan hai: distance over time. Par 'abhi' ek single instant hai, aur ek instant mein koi time guzarta hi nahin.

To lagta hai hum change over zero nikaal rahe hain — bekaar. Phir bhi speedometer confidently jawaab deta hai. Uski trick: ek chhote se time ke sliver par distance naapo aur divide karo, phir sliver ko chhota se chhota karte jao.
Jaise time-window zero ki taraf simatti hai, wo average-over-a-sliver ek single definite number par aa jaata hai — aapki instantaneous speed. Yahi limiting process bilkul derivative hai.

Yahi idea poori tarah geometric hai. Curve ke do points ko ek secant line se jodiye — uska slope un dono ke beech ka average rate hai. Ab doosre point ko pehle ki taraf slide kijiye: secant ghoomta hai jab tak wo tangent na ban jaaye jo curve ko bas chhoo kar guzarti hai.

Dono pictures ko formalise karne se milta hai first principle, jise ab-initio ya delta method bhi kehte hain. Derivative f dash of x hai limit, jaise h zero ki taraf jaaye, of f of x plus h minus f of x, bata h.
Tukda-tukda padhiye: numerator hai output mein change; denominator ka h hai input ka simatta hua sliver. Slope of tangent aur instantaneous rate, is ek expression ke do chehre hain.
Aur gaur kijiye ye asal mein hai kya — ek zero over zero limit. Limits aur standard limits ke baare mein jo aapne seekha, wahi machinery derivatives ko chalati hai.
Ek aur baat. F dash ek single point a par ek number hai — ek slope. Par derivative ko har point par evaluate kijiye aur aapko milta hai ek bilkul naya function, f dash of x.

sections.title: When does a derivative fail to exist?

board_events.text: When does a derivative fail to exist?
$f'(a)$ exists $\iff$ LHD $=$ RHD.

board_events.text: A jump or a vertical tangent also kills the derivative.
But continuous does NOT imply differentiable — $|x|$ at $0$ is the counterexample.
$f'(a)$ is a number; $f'(x)$ is a function — do not leave an $x$ where a number belongs.

segments.text: A derivative is a limit, so it can fail exactly the way limits fail. Let us see the four situations that kill it.

First, the limit must exist. The derivative at a exists only if the two one-sided difference quotients agree — the left-hand derivative equals the right-hand derivative. That is the same existence rule from limits, applied to the difference quotient.

Second, smoothness is required. A sharp corner, like the absolute value of x at zero, has a left slope of minus one and a right slope of plus one. They disagree, so no tangent, and no derivative — even though the function is perfectly defined there.
It is not only corners. A jump in the graph, or a vertical tangent where the slope runs off to infinity, will each kill the derivative just as surely.
Third, a crucial one-way street. If f is differentiable at a, it must be continuous there. Differentiability forces continuity.
But the reverse absolutely fails. Continuity alone is not enough — the absolute value of x is continuous everywhere yet not differentiable at zero. The arrow points one way only.
And a bookkeeping point boards penalise: f dash at a is a single number, a slope at one point; f dash of x is a whole function. Never leave an x sitting where a number belongs.
Derivative ek limit hai, to ye theek waise fail ho sakta hai jaise limits fail hoti hain. Chaliye wo chaar situations dekhte hain jo ise khatm kar deti hain.

Pehla, limit ka exist karna zaroori hai. Derivative at a tabhi exist karta hai jab dono one-sided difference quotients agree karein — left-hand derivative barabar right-hand derivative. Ye wahi existence rule hai limits wala, difference quotient par lagaya hua.

Doosra, smoothness zaroori hai. Ek sharp corner, jaise absolute value of x zero par, ka left slope hai minus one aur right slope hai plus one. Ye disagree karte hain, to koi tangent nahin, aur koi derivative nahin — bhale hi function wahan bilkul defined ho.
Sirf corners hi nahin. Graph mein ek jump, ya ek vertical tangent jahan slope infinity tak bhaag jaaye, har ek derivative ko utni hi pakke tarah khatm kar deta hai.
Teesra, ek zaroori one-way street. Agar f, a par differentiable hai, to wahan continuous hona hi chahiye. Differentiability continuity ko force karti hai.
Par ulta bilkul fail hota hai. Sirf continuity kaafi nahin — absolute value of x har jagah continuous hai phir bhi zero par differentiable nahin. Arrow sirf ek taraf point karta hai.

Aur ek bookkeeping point jispar boards penalise karte hain: f dash at a ek single number hai, ek point par slope; f dash of x ek poora function hai. Kabhi ek x wahan mat chhodiye jahan number aana chahiye.

sections.title: Deriving the standard results from scratch

board_events.text: Deriving the standard results from scratch
For the product rule, add and subtract the cross term $u(x+h)v(x)$.
Every first-principle derivation aims to manufacture a standard limit.

segments.text: Let us actually run the first-principle machine on the big three — x to the n, sine x, and e to the x — and see why the product rule looks the way it does.

The procedure is always the same four steps: write f of x plus h, form the difference quotient, simplify the numerator so the h in the denominator can be handled, then take the limit as h goes to zero.

For x to the n, use the point-form of the definition. It is literally the star limit from the first subtopic, with a replaced by x — so the derivative is n x to the n minus one, with no new work at all.

For sine x, use the identity sine of x plus h minus sine x equals two cosine of x plus h over two, times sine h over two. The sine h over two, over h over two, is a standard limit tending to one, and cosine collapses to cosine x.

For e to the x, factor the base function out of the difference quotient. What is left is e to the h minus one over h — the exponential junction, equal to one. So e to the x is its own derivative, the famous self-replicating property.
The product rule needs one clever step. In the difference quotient for u times v, add and subtract the cross term u of x plus h, times v of x. That splits the numerator into two clean pieces.
Take the limit of each piece and you land on u v dash plus v u dash. That leftover cross term is exactly why two derivatives cannot simply multiply.

Notice the single strategy underneath all three: your one goal is always to manufacture a standard limit — a sine over angle, or an e to the h minus one over h — and the junction hands you the answer.
Chaliye first-principle machine ko asal mein chalate hain teen badon par — x to the n, sine x, aur e to the x — aur dekhte hain product rule aisa kyun dikhta hai.

Procedure hamesha wahi chaar steps hai: f of x plus h likhiye, difference quotient banaiye, numerator ko simplify kijiye taaki denominator ka h handle ho sake, phir limit lijiye jaise h zero ki taraf jaaye.

X to the n ke liye, definition ka point-form istemaal kijiye. Ye literally pehle subtopic wali star limit hai, a ki jagah x ke saath — to derivative hai n x to the n minus one, bina kisi naye kaam ke.

Sine x ke liye, identity istemaal kijiye: sine of x plus h minus sine x barabar two cosine of x plus h over two, into sine h over two. Sine h over two, over h over two, ek standard limit hai jo one ki taraf jaati hai, aur cosine simat kar cosine x ban jaata hai.

E to the x ke liye, base function ko difference quotient mein se factor kar lijiye. Jo bachta hai wo hai e to the h minus one over h — exponential junction, barabar one. To e to the x apna hi derivative hai, wo mashhoor self-replicating property.
Product rule ko ek clever step chahiye. U times v ke difference quotient mein, cross term u of x plus h, into v of x ko add aur subtract kijiye. Ye numerator ko do saaf pieces mein baant deta hai.
Har piece ki limit lijiye aur aap pahunchte hain u v dash plus v u dash par. Wahi bacha hua cross term theek wo wajah hai ki do derivatives yun hi multiply nahin ho sakte.
Teenon ke neeche ek hi strategy dekhiye: aapka ek maqsad hamesha hai ek standard limit banaana — ek sine over angle, ya ek e to the h minus one over h — aur junction aapko answer de deta hai.

sections.title: Definitions, notations, and the standard set

board_events.text: Definitions, notations, and the standard set
Notations $f'(x)$, $\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)]$, $Df$ all mean the same thing.

board_events.latex: \dfrac{d}{dx}x^{n} = n x^{n-1}, \quad \dfrac{d}{dx}e^{x} = e^{x}, \quad \dfrac{d}{dx}a^{x} = a^{x}\ln a, \quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln x = \dfrac{1}{x}
\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x, \quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x, \quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^{2} x

board_events.text: Each is provable from first principle; how they combine across $+,-,\times,\div$ is the next subtopic.
Existence: $f'(a)$ exists $\iff$ LHD $=$ RHD. Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous.

segments.text: Here is the derivative toolkit for quick recall — both forms of the definition, the notations, and the standard results.
The definition comes in two equivalent forms — the h-form with x plus h, and the point-form with t approaching x. Use whichever fits the problem.
Four notations all mean exactly the same thing — f dash of x, d y by d x, d by d x of f of x, and capital D f. Do not let the different symbols confuse you.

Two interpretations to hold together. Geometrically, f dash at a is the slope of the tangent, that is tangent of the angle psi. Physically, if s of t is position, then s dash of t is the instantaneous velocity.
The power and exponential standard results — derivative of x to the n is n x to the n minus one; e to the x is its own derivative; a to the x gives a to the x times log a; and log x gives one over x.
The core trigonometric results — derivative of sine x is cosine x; derivative of cosine x is minus sine x; and derivative of tangent x is secant squared x.
Every one of these is provable straight from first principle. And how they combine across plus, minus, times, and divide is the business of the next subtopic — the rules of differentiation.
And stamped over all of it, the existence rule — f dash at a exists exactly when the left-hand and right-hand derivatives agree, and differentiable always implies continuous.
Ye rahi derivative toolkit quick recall ke liye — definition ke dono forms, notations, aur standard results.
Definition do equivalent forms mein aati hai — h-form x plus h ke saath, aur point-form t approaching x ke saath. Jo problem mein fit ho wo istemaal kijiye.
Chaar notations sabka matlab bilkul ek hi hai — f dash of x, d y by d x, d by d x of f of x, aur capital D f. Alag symbols aapko confuse na karein.
Do interpretations saath rakhiye. Geometrically, f dash at a hai tangent ka slope, yaani tangent of the angle psi. Physically, agar s of t position hai, to s dash of t hai instantaneous velocity.

Power aur exponential standard results — derivative of x to the n hai n x to the n minus one; e to the x apna hi derivative hai; a to the x deta hai a to the x into log a; aur log x deta hai one over x.
Core trigonometric results — derivative of sine x hai cosine x; derivative of cosine x hai minus sine x; aur derivative of tangent x hai secant squared x.
Inmein se har ek seedhe first principle se provable hai. Aur ye plus, minus, times, aur divide ke across kaise combine hote hain, wo agle subtopic ka kaam hai — rules of differentiation.
Aur in sab par chhapa hua, existence rule — f dash at a tabhi exist karta hai jab left-hand aur right-hand derivatives agree karein, aur differentiable hamesha continuous ko imply karta hai.

sections.title: Derivative of √x, and a disguised derivative

board_events.text: Worked example: derivative of √x from first principle
Difference quotient $\frac{\sqrt{x+h}-\sqrt{x}}{h}$ gives $\frac{0}{0}$ at $h=0$.
Speed trap: a disguised derivative
This is exactly $f'(2)$ for $f(x)=x^{10}$ — do not expand the binomial.
Any limit shaped like $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ is a derivative — read off $f'(a)$.

segments.text: Find the derivative of f of x equals root x, straight from first principle.
Steps one and two, form the difference quotient: root of x plus h, minus root x, all over h. Substituting h equals zero gives zero over zero — a surd, so rationalise.
Step three, multiply by the conjugate. The numerator becomes x plus h minus x, which is just h, and that h cancels the h in the denominator, leaving one over root of x plus h, plus root x.
Step four, take the limit. As h goes to zero the two roots become equal, giving one over two root x. That is the derivative of root x, consistent with treating it as x to the half.
<curious>Now spot the disguise.</curious> Evaluate the limit as h goes to zero of two plus h, all to the ten, minus two to the ten, over h.
The trap is to start binomially expanding two plus h to the ten — minutes lost. Recognise the shape: this is precisely the first-principle definition of f dash at two for f of x equals x to the ten.
So just read it off. f dash at two is ten times two to the nine, which is ten times five hundred twelve, which is five thousand one hundred twenty.
<whisper>Lock in the reflex.</whisper> Any limit shaped like f of a plus h, minus f of a, over h is a derivative in disguise — identify the function and read off f dash at a, never grind.
F of x barabar root x ka derivative nikaliye, seedhe first principle se.
Steps one aur two, difference quotient banaiye: root of x plus h, minus root x, bata h. H barabar zero rakhne par zero over zero milta hai — ek surd, to rationalise kijiye.
Step three, conjugate se multiply kijiye. Numerator ban jaata hai x plus h minus x, yaani sirf h, aur wo h denominator ke h ko cancel kar deta hai, bachta hai one over root of x plus h, plus root x.
Step four, limit lijiye. Jaise h zero ki taraf jaaye dono roots barabar ho jaate hain, milta hai one over two root x. Yahi root x ka derivative hai, x to the half maanne ke saath consistent.
<curious>Ab bhes pehchaniye.</curious> Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise h zero ki taraf jaaye, of two plus h, all to the ten, minus two to the ten, bata h.
Trap hai two plus h to the ten ko binomially expand karne lagna — minutes barbaad. Shape pehchaniye: ye theek f dash at two ki first-principle definition hai, f of x barabar x to the ten ke liye.
To bas padh lijiye. F dash at two hai ten into two to the nine, yaani ten into five hundred twelve, yaani five thousand one hundred twenty.

<whisper>Reflex pakka kar lijiye.</whisper> Koi bhi limit jiska shape ho f of a plus h, minus f of a, bata h, wo bhes badla derivative hai — function pehchaniye aur f dash at a padh lijiye, kabhi grind mat kijiye.

sections.title: Derivative of aˣ, and differentiability at an oscillating point

board_events.text: Worked example: derivative of aˣ from first principle
Set $a=e$: since $\ln e = 1$, this recovers $\frac{d}{dx}e^{x}=e^{x}$ — a clean check.
Advanced: differentiability at an oscillating point
Differentiable here, yet $f'$ is not continuous at $0$ — an Advanced favourite.

segments.text: Find the derivative of f of x equals a to the x, with a positive, from first principle.
Form the difference quotient and factor out the base function a to the x. What remains is a to the h minus one over h.
That remaining limit is exactly the exponential junction from the standard limits, equal to log a. So the derivative of a to the x is a to the x times log a.
A satisfying self-check: set a equal to e. Since log of e is one, this collapses to e to the x, exactly matching our earlier result. The pieces fit.
Now a subtle advanced one. Let f of x be x squared sine of one over x for x not zero, and zero at x equals zero. Show f is differentiable at zero and find f dash at zero.

Sine of one over x oscillates wildly near zero, so you cannot just plug in. Go to the definition at the point: f dash at zero is the limit of h squared sine one over h, over h, which simplifies to h times sine one over h.

Now squeeze. Since sine of one over h is between minus one and one, h times it is trapped between minus mod h and plus mod h. Both bounds go to zero, so by the Sandwich Theorem f dash at zero is zero.
The deep point, and a favourite advanced trap: f is differentiable at zero, yet its derivative is not continuous there. Differentiable does not imply continuously differentiable.
F of x barabar a to the x, a positive ke saath, ka derivative nikaliye first principle se.
Difference quotient banaiye aur base function a to the x ko factor kar lijiye. Jo bachta hai wo hai a to the h minus one over h.
Wo bacha hua limit theek exponential junction hai standard limits wala, barabar log a. To a to the x ka derivative hai a to the x into log a.
Ek santoshjanak self-check: a ko e ke barabar rakhiye. Kyunki log of e one hai, ye simat kar e to the x ban jaata hai, hamare pehle wale result se bilkul match. Tukde fit baithte hain.
Ab ek subtle advanced. Maan lijiye f of x hai x squared sine of one over x jab x zero nahin, aur zero jab x barabar zero. Dikhaiye f, zero par differentiable hai aur f dash at zero nikaliye.

Sine of one over x zero ke paas bahut oscillate karta hai, to aap bas plug in nahin kar sakte. Point par definition par jaiye: f dash at zero hai limit of h squared sine one over h, bata h, jo simplify hokar banta hai h into sine one over h.

Ab squeeze kijiye. Kyunki sine of one over h, minus one aur one ke beech hai, h into wo, minus mod h aur plus mod h ke beech phansa hai. Dono bounds zero ki taraf jaate hain, to Sandwich Theorem se f dash at zero hai zero.
Gehra point, aur ek favourite advanced trap: f, zero par differentiable hai, phir bhi uska derivative wahan continuous nahin. Differentiable ka matlab continuously differentiable nahin hota.

sections.title: Traps: f'(a) vs f'(x), the product rule, cancelling h, continuity

board_events.text: Four traps in first-principle work
Trap 1: mixing up $f'(a)$ (a number) with $f'(x)$ (a function).
Trap 2: the wrong product rule — $(uv)' \neq u'v'$.
Trap 3: cancelling $h$ too early, or dropping the $\lim_{h\to 0}$ step.
Trap 4: assuming continuous $\Rightarrow$ differentiable. It is one-way.
Pro-tip: a limit shaped $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ is $f'(a)$ — never expand.
In any sin/cos/eˣ derivation, manufacture a standard limit — the junction appears.

segments.text: Four traps trip students in derivatives from first principle. Let us name each one.
Trap one, mixing up f dash at a with f dash of x. The first is a single number, a slope at one point; the second is a whole new function. Boards penalise leaving an x where a number belongs.
Trap two, the wrong product rule. u v whole dash is not u dash v dash. It is u dash v plus u v dash — the cross term is non-negotiable.

Trap three, cancelling h too early or skipping the limit. You may only cancel h after simplifying the numerator, and you must still write the limit as h goes to zero — dropping it loses method marks and hides errors.
Trap four, assuming continuous implies differentiable. It runs one way only. Corners like mod x, cusps, and vertical tangents are all continuous but not differentiable.
<whisper>Train your eye for the disguise.</whisper> Any limit shaped like f of a plus h minus f of a, over h, or f of x minus f of a over x minus a, is just f dash at a. Never expand it by hand.
And in every first-principle derivation of a sine, cosine, or e to the x, your single goal is to manufacture a standard limit. Factor out the base function and the junction appears on its own.
Chaar traps students ko first-principle derivatives mein giraate hain. Chaliye har ek ko naam dete hain.

Trap one, f dash at a ko f dash of x se milaana. Pehla ek single number hai, ek point par slope; doosra ek poora naya function hai. Boards penalise karte hain jab aap x wahan chhod dein jahan number aana chahiye.
Trap two, galat product rule. U v whole dash, u dash v dash nahin hota. Ye hai u dash v plus u v dash — cross term non-negotiable hai.

Trap three, h ko bahut jaldi cancel karna ya limit chhod dena. Aap h ko sirf numerator simplify karne ke baad cancel kar sakte hain, aur aapko phir bhi limit as h goes to zero likhna hi hoga — use chhodna method marks kha jaata hai aur galtiyaan chhupaata hai.
Trap four, ye maan lena ki continuous ka matlab differentiable. Ye sirf ek taraf chalta hai. Corners jaise mod x, cusps, aur vertical tangents sab continuous hain par differentiable nahin.

<whisper>Bhes ke liye aankh tez kijiye.</whisper> Koi bhi limit jiska shape ho f of a plus h minus f of a, bata h, ya f of x minus f of a over x minus a, wo bas f dash at a hai. Kabhi haath se expand mat kijiye.
Aur sine, cosine, ya e to the x ki har first-principle derivation mein, aapka ek maqsad hai ek standard limit banaana. Base function ko factor kijiye aur junction khud-ba-khud saamne aa jaata hai.

Addition is friendly — derivatives just add. Multiplication is the first surprise.

Chain rule needs both links differentiable — inner $g$ at $x$, outer $f$ at $u$.
And do not reach for a rule when algebra is faster — simplify first.

segments.text: <curious>In the last subtopic you ground out derivatives the honest way, straight from the limit.</curious> It works, but it is slow — like grinding wheat into atta by hand. This subtopic is the flour mill.
Once a few key results are proven from first principle, we switch to a small set of rules. Every rule answers exactly one question — how does the derivative interact with an arithmetic operation?

Addition is friendly: derivatives simply add. But multiplication is the first surprise — derivatives do not just multiply. The correct law is the product rule, u dash v plus u v dash, because of the leftover cross term.
Division has its own quotient rule. And composition — a function inside another function — is the subtlest and most powerful: the chain rule, d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x.

The chain rule intuitively: rates multiply. If y changes three times as fast as u, and u changes twice as fast as x, then y changes six times as fast as x. Picture a gear train — the gear ratios simply multiply.
Or think of currency: rupees per dollar, times dollars per euro, gives rupees per euro. The intermediate unit cancels, and the rates chain. That cancelling is exactly d y by d u times d u by d x.

The chain rule has a condition: both links must be differentiable — the inner function g at x, and the outer function f at u equals g of x. And the quotient rule always needs the denominator non-zero at the point.
One habit above all the rules — do not reach for a rule when plain algebra is faster. If an expression simplifies first, simplify, then differentiate. It often turns a slog into one line.

<curious>Pichhle subtopic mein aapne derivatives imaandaari se nikaale, seedhe limit se.</curious> Ye kaam karta hai, par slow hai — haath se gehun ko atta peesne jaisa. Ye subtopic wo aata chakki hai.

Ek baar kuch key results first principle se prove ho jaayein, hum ek chhote se rules ke set par switch karte hain. Har rule theek ek sawaal ka jawaab deta hai — derivative kisi arithmetic operation ke saath kaise interact karta hai?

Addition friendly hai: derivatives bas jud jaate hain. Par multiplication pehla surprise hai — derivatives yun hi multiply nahin hote. Sahi law hai product rule, u dash v plus u v dash, us bache hue cross term ki wajah se.
Division ka apna quotient rule hai. Aur composition — ek function doosre function ke andar — sabse subtle aur powerful hai: chain rule, d y by d x barabar d y by d u into d u by d x.

Chain rule intuitively: rates multiply karte hain. Agar y, u se teen guna tez badalta hai, aur u, x se do guna tez, to y, x se chhe guna tez badalta hai. Ek gear train sochiye — gear ratios bas multiply ho jaate hain.

Ya currency sochiye: rupees per dollar, into dollars per euro, deta hai rupees per euro. Beech ki unit cancel ho jaati hai, aur rates chain ho jaate hain. Wahi cancelling theek d y by d u into d u by d x hai.

Chain rule ki ek condition hai: dono links differentiable hone chahiye — inner function g at x, aur outer function f at u barabar g of x. Aur quotient rule ko hamesha point par denominator non-zero chahiye.
Sab rules se upar ek aadat — rule mat uthaiye jab simple algebra tez ho. Agar expression pehle simplify hoti hai, simplify kijiye, phir differentiate. Ye aksar ek slog ko ek line bana deta hai.

sections.title: How the rules interlock

board_events.text: How the rules interlock

board_events.latex: y = \dfrac{u}{v} \;\Rightarrow\; u = yv \;\Rightarrow\; u' = y'v + yv'
\dfrac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x, \qquad \dfrac{d}{dx}\csc x = -\csc x\cot x
\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \cdot \dfrac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}

board_events.text: As $\Delta x \to 0$, $\Delta u \to 0$ too, and each factor tends to its derivative.
To differentiate anything: simplify, spot the outermost operation, then peel outside-in.

segments.text: The rules are not a random list — they lock into each other. Let us derive the quotient rule from the product rule, and complete the trig table.
Start with y equals u over v, so u equals y v. Differentiate both sides by the product rule: u dash equals y dash v plus y v dash. We will just solve this for y dash.

Solve for y dash and substitute y equals u over v. After tidying, you get u dash v minus u v dash, all over v squared. The quotient rule is just the product rule rearranged — which is why the order and the minus sign matter.

Now complete the trig table. For cotangent x, which is cosine over sine, the quotient rule gives minus sine squared plus cosine squared, over sine squared — that is minus one over sine squared, which is minus cosecant squared x.
The reciprocal rule on secant, which is one over cosine, gives secant x times tangent x. Identically, cosecant x gives minus cosecant x times cotangent x. That closes the full set of six.
For the chain rule, look at average rates over a small step and insert the intermediate change delta u. The ratio delta y over delta x equals delta y over delta u, times delta u over delta x.

As delta x heads to zero, delta u heads to zero too, because the inner function is continuous. Each factor tends to its derivative, giving the chain rule. The cancelling-rates picture is the right intuition.

So the master procedure. Simplify first if you can, then identify the outermost operation — sum, product, quotient, or composition — apply that rule, and for compositions peel outside-in, layer by layer, until you reach x.
Rules koi random list nahin — ye ek-doosre mein lock hote hain. Chaliye quotient rule ko product rule se derive karte hain, aur trig table complete karte hain.
Shuru kijiye y barabar u over v se, to u barabar y v. Dono sides ko product rule se differentiate kijiye: u dash barabar y dash v plus y v dash. Hum bas ise y dash ke liye solve karenge.

Y dash ke liye solve kijiye aur y barabar u over v rakhiye. Tidy karne ke baad, milta hai u dash v minus u v dash, bata v squared. Quotient rule bas product rule ka rearrange hai — isiliye order aur minus sign maayne rakhte hain.

Ab trig table complete kijiye. Cotangent x ke liye, jo cosine over sine hai, quotient rule deta hai minus sine squared plus cosine squared, bata sine squared — yaani minus one over sine squared, jo hai minus cosecant squared x.
Reciprocal rule secant par, jo one over cosine hai, deta hai secant x into tangent x. Waise hi, cosecant x deta hai minus cosecant x into cotangent x. Ye chhaho ka poora set band kar deta hai.
Chain rule ke liye, ek chhote step par average rates dekhiye aur beech ka change delta u daaliye. Ratio delta y over delta x barabar delta y over delta u, into delta u over delta x.

Jaise delta x zero ki taraf jaaye, delta u bhi zero ki taraf jaata hai, kyunki inner function continuous hai. Har factor apne derivative ki taraf jaata hai, chain rule dekar. Cancelling-rates wali picture sahi intuition hai.

To master procedure. Pehle simplify kijiye agar ho sake, phir outermost operation pehchaniye — sum, product, quotient, ya composition — wo rule lagaiye, aur compositions ke liye outside-in peel kijiye, layer dar layer, jab tak x tak na pahunch jaayein.

sections.title: The complete rule set

board_events.text: The complete rule set

board_events.latex: \dfrac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x, \qquad \dfrac{d}{dx}\csc x = -\csc x\cot x

board_events.text: Simplify before differentiating whenever you can — it saves the most time.

segments.text: Here are all the differentiation rules in one place, plus the toolkit of standard derivatives they act on.
The friendly ones first — the derivative of a sum or difference is the sum or difference of derivatives, and a constant multiple pulls straight out.
The product rule — u dash v plus u v dash, always two terms. For three factors, differentiate one at a time and add: u dash v w, plus u v dash w, plus u v w dash.
The quotient rule — u dash v minus u v dash, all over v squared, valid only where v is not zero. Note the order: top-derivative-times-bottom comes first, and swapping it flips the sign.
The chain rule — d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x. Its most-used special case is the power chain rule: n times g to the n minus one, times g dash of x.
The tangent and cotangent results — derivative of tangent x is secant squared x, and derivative of cotangent x is minus cosecant squared x.
And the reciprocal pair — derivative of secant x is secant x times tangent x, and derivative of cosecant x is minus cosecant x times cotangent x. That is the full set of six trig derivatives.
Stamped over the whole set, the one habit that saves the most time — simplify before you differentiate whenever you possibly can.
Ye rahe saare differentiation rules ek jagah, saath mein standard derivatives ki toolkit jinpar ye act karte hain.
Pehle friendly wale — sum ya difference ka derivative hai derivatives ka sum ya difference, aur constant multiple seedha bahar aa jaata hai.
Product rule — u dash v plus u v dash, hamesha do terms. Teen factors ke liye, ek-ek karke differentiate karke jodiye: u dash v w, plus u v dash w, plus u v w dash.
Quotient rule — u dash v minus u v dash, bata v squared, sirf wahan valid jahan v zero na ho. Order note kijiye: top-derivative-into-bottom pehle aata hai, aur ise swap karne se sign palat jaata hai.
Chain rule — d y by d x barabar d y by d u into d u by d x. Iska sabse zyada istemaal hone wala special case hai power chain rule: n into g to the n minus one, into g dash of x.
Tangent aur cotangent results — derivative of tangent x hai secant squared x, aur derivative of cotangent x hai minus cosecant squared x.
Aur reciprocal pair — derivative of secant x hai secant x into tangent x, aur derivative of cosecant x hai minus cosecant x into cotangent x. Ye poora set hai chhe trig derivatives ka.
Poore set par chhapa hua, wo ek aadat jo sabse zyada time bachaati hai — differentiate karne se pehle jab bhi mumkin ho, simplify kijiye.

board_events.text: Speed trap: simplify before you differentiate
Always ask: can I simplify before I differentiate?

segments.text: Differentiate y equals x cubed sine x — a clean product of two functions.
Step one, identify the two factors. Let u be x cubed and v be sine x. Naming them first keeps the product rule tidy.
Their derivatives are quick: u dash is three x squared, and v dash is cosine x.
Apply u dash v plus u v dash: three x squared sine x, plus x cubed cosine x. Factor out x squared and it tidies into x squared times three sine x plus x cosine x.
<curious>Now the trap of reaching for a rule too fast.</curious> Differentiate y equals x squared plus one, all over x.
Students immediately fire the quotient rule — slow and error-prone. Instead, simplify first: x squared plus one, over x, is just x plus x to the minus one.
Now differentiate term by term: one, minus x to the minus two, which is one minus one over x squared. A quotient-rule slog became a single clean line.
<whisper>Make it a habit.</whisper> Before firing any rule, always ask — can I simplify first? It often turns a heavy computation into one line.
Differentiate kijiye y barabar x cubed sine x — do functions ka ek saaf product.
Step one, do factors pehchaniye. Maan lijiye u hai x cubed aur v hai sine x. Inhein pehle naam dena product rule ko saaf rakhta hai.
Inke derivatives jhat se: u dash hai three x squared, aur v dash hai cosine x.
U dash v plus u v dash lagaiye: three x squared sine x, plus x cubed cosine x. X squared ko factor kijiye aur ye tidy hokar banta hai x squared into three sine x plus x cosine x.
<curious>Ab rule ko bahut jaldi uthaane ka trap.</curious> Differentiate kijiye y barabar x squared plus one, bata x.
Students turant quotient rule chala dete hain — slow aur error-prone. Iske bajaay pehle simplify kijiye: x squared plus one, bata x, bas x plus x to the minus one hai.
Ab term-by-term differentiate kijiye: one, minus x to the minus two, yaani one minus one over x squared. Ek quotient-rule slog ek saaf line ban gaya.
<whisper>Ise aadat banaiye.</whisper> Koi bhi rule chalaane se pehle, hamesha poochhiye — kya main pehle simplify kar sakta hoon? Ye aksar ek bhaari computation ko ek line bana deta hai.
