board_events.text: Worked example: product rule meets chain rule
It's a product of $u = x^{2}$ and $v = \cos(3x)$; $v$ needs the chain rule.
Advanced: three nested layers
Outermost $\sin(\square)$ gives $\cos(\square)$, keeping $\square = \cos(x^{2})$ intact.
Next $\cos(x^{2}) \to -\sin(x^{2})$; innermost $x^{2} \to 2x$.

segments.text: Differentiate y equals x squared cosine of three x — this combines the product rule with the chain rule.
It is a product of u equals x squared and v equals cosine of three x. The x squared part is easy, but v itself is a composition, so v dash needs the chain rule.
For v dash, peel the chain: the outer cosine becomes minus sine, keeping three x intact, times the derivative of the inside, which is three. So v dash is minus three sine of three x.
Now the product rule, u dash v plus u v dash: two x cosine three x, plus x squared times minus three sine three x. That gives two x cosine three x, minus three x squared sine three x.
Now three nested layers. Differentiate y equals sine of cosine of x squared. Peel strictly from the outside in.
The outermost layer is sine of a box; its derivative is cosine of the box, with the box, cosine of x squared, kept completely intact. That is layer one.
The next layer, derivative of cosine of x squared, is minus sine of x squared, times the derivative of x squared. And the innermost, derivative of x squared, is two x.

Multiply the whole chain of three: cosine of cosine x squared, times minus sine x squared, times two x. Tidied, that is minus two x sine of x squared, times cosine of cosine of x squared. One missed inner derivative and the whole answer is wrong.
Differentiate kijiye y barabar x squared cosine of three x — ye product rule ko chain rule ke saath combine karta hai.
Ye ek product hai u barabar x squared aur v barabar cosine of three x. X squared part aasaan hai, par v khud ek composition hai, to v dash ko chain rule chahiye.
V dash ke liye, chain peel kijiye: outer cosine banta hai minus sine, three x ko intact rakhte hue, into inside ka derivative, jo hai three. To v dash hai minus three sine of three x.
Ab product rule, u dash v plus u v dash: two x cosine three x, plus x squared into minus three sine three x. Milta hai two x cosine three x, minus three x squared sine three x.
Ab teen nested layers. Differentiate kijiye y barabar sine of cosine of x squared. Sakhti se outside se andar ki taraf peel kijiye.
Outermost layer hai sine of a box; iska derivative hai cosine of the box, box ko, cosine of x squared, poori tarah intact rakhte hue. Ye layer one.
Agli layer, derivative of cosine of x squared, hai minus sine of x squared, into x squared ka derivative. Aur innermost, derivative of x squared, hai two x.

Teenon ki poori chain multiply kijiye: cosine of cosine x squared, into minus sine x squared, into two x. Tidy karke, ye hai minus two x sine of x squared, into cosine of cosine of x squared. Ek inner derivative chhoota aur poora answer galat.

sections.title: Traps: inner derivative, product rule, quotient order, simplification

board_events.text: The four rule-of-differentiation traps
Trap 1: forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule.
Trap 2: the wrong product rule — $(uv)' \neq u'v'$, always two terms.
Trap 3: quotient-rule order and sign — $u'v$ first, then minus $uv'$.
Trap 4: skipping simplification and grinding an unsimplified expression.
Pro-tip: 'outside derivative, inside kept whole, times inside derivative' — repeat per layer.
For three-or-more-factor products, differentiate one factor at a time and add.

segments.text: Four traps ambush students once the rules are in hand. Let us name each.

Trap one, and the most common of all — forgetting the inner derivative. Derivative of sine of x squared is not cosine of x squared; it is two x cosine of x squared. Every composition contributes a times-derivative-of-the-inside.
Trap two, the wrong product rule again. u v whole dash is not u dash v dash. It is u dash v plus u v dash — always two terms.
Trap three, quotient-rule order and sign. The numerator is u dash v minus u v dash — top-derivative-times-bottom first. Reverse it and both the sign and the answer flip.
Trap four, skipping simplification. Differentiating an unsimplified quotient or product wastes time and multiplies your chances of error. Simplify, then differentiate.

<whisper>The chain-rule mantra.</whisper> Say it for every composition — derivative of the outside with the inside kept whole, times the derivative of the inside — and repeat, layer by layer, until you hit x.
And for products of three or more factors, do not try to group them — just differentiate one factor at a time, keeping the others fixed, and add the results.
Chaar traps students par ghaat lagaate hain jab rules haath mein aa jaate hain. Chaliye har ek ko naam dete hain.

Trap one, aur sabse common — inner derivative bhoolna. Derivative of sine of x squared, cosine of x squared nahin hai; ye hai two x cosine of x squared. Har composition ek into-derivative-of-the-inside deta hai.
Trap two, phir se galat product rule. U v whole dash, u dash v dash nahin. Ye hai u dash v plus u v dash — hamesha do terms.
Trap three, quotient-rule order aur sign. Numerator hai u dash v minus u v dash — top-derivative-into-bottom pehle. Ise ulta kijiye aur sign aur answer dono palat jaate hain.
Trap four, simplification chhodna. Ek unsimplified quotient ya product ko differentiate karna time barbaad karta hai aur error ke chances badhaata hai. Simplify kijiye, phir differentiate.

<whisper>Chain-rule mantra.</whisper> Har composition ke liye kahiye — derivative of the outside, inside ko whole rakhte hue, into derivative of the inside — aur dohraiye, layer dar layer, jab tak x tak na pahunchein.
Aur teen ya zyada factors ke products ke liye, unhein group karne ki koshish mat kijiye — bas ek-ek factor differentiate kijiye, baaki ko fixed rakhte hue, aur results jod dijiye.

The greatest integer function $[x]$ is the classic exam vehicle for one-sided limits.

segments.text: <curious>So far every limit asked the same question: as x creeps to a finite point, what finite value does f approach?</curious> Two situations escape that mould, and a complete picture needs both.
First, end behaviour — where does f head as x runs off to infinity? Picture zooming out on a graph until the fine detail vanishes and only the overall trend remains.

For a rational function far out, the small terms become irrelevant — only the highest powers on top and bottom matter, and their ratio is the limit. It is like the single two-thousand-rupee note deciding your wallet's value, no matter how many coins rattle alongside.
So three x squared plus five, over six x squared minus x, settles toward three over six, which is one-half. Everything except the leading terms is noise that one over x washes away.

The second situation — the limit can simply fail at a jump, or run off to infinity. Think of an autorickshaw fare meter, or electricity billed in slabs: the charge holds flat, then jumps at each boundary.

Here are both pictures side by side. On the left, a rational function flattening toward the horizontal line y equals one-half. On the right, the greatest integer function — a staircase, with a filled dot on the left of each step and an open dot on the right.

Approach a boundary from the left and you read the lower slab; approach from the right and you read the higher one. The two disagree, so there is no single value being approached — the limit does not exist at the jump.
The greatest integer function, written box x — the largest integer at most x — is exactly this staircase, and it is the classic exam vehicle for testing whether you truly understand one-sided limits.

<curious>Ab tak har limit ek hi sawaal poochhti thi: jaise x kisi finite point tak pahunche, f kis finite value ki taraf jaata hai?</curious> Do situations is dhaanche se bach nikalti hain, aur poori tasveer ke liye dono chahiye.
Pehli, end behaviour — f kahaan jaata hai jaise x infinity ki taraf bhaage? Graph ko zoom out karke sochiye jab tak baareek detail gaayab na ho jaaye aur sirf overall trend bache.

Ek rational function ke liye door tak, chhote terms irrelevant ho jaate hain — sirf upar aur neeche ki highest powers maayne rakhti hain, aur unka ratio hi limit hai. Jaise wallet mein ek do-hazaar ka note uski value tay karta hai, chaahe kitne hi sikke saath khanke.
To three x squared plus five, bata six x squared minus x, aa jaata hai three over six ki taraf, yaani one-half. Leading terms ke alaawa sab kuch noise hai jise one over x dho deta hai.

Doosri situation — limit kisi jump par bas fail ho sakti hai, ya infinity tak bhaag sakti hai. Ek auto ke fare meter ko sochiye, ya bijli ka bill slabs mein: charge flat rehta hai, phir har boundary par jump kar jaata hai.

Ye rahi dono tasveerein saath-saath. Baayin taraf, ek rational function jo y barabar one-half ki horizontal line ki taraf flat hota hai. Daayin taraf, greatest integer function — ek staircase, har step ke baayin par bhara dot aur daayin par khula dot.

Boundary ko baayin se approach kijiye to lower slab padhte hain; daayin se approach kijiye to higher. Dono disagree karte hain, to koi ek value approach nahin ho rahi — jump par limit exist nahin karti.

Greatest integer function, box x likha jaata hai — x se chhota ya barabar sabse bada integer — yahi staircase hai, aur ye classic exam vehicle hai ye test karne ke liye ki aap one-sided limits sach mein samajhte hain.

board_events.text: Handling infinity, and jumps, without mistakes
$\infty$ is a direction, not a number — $\infty-\infty$ and $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$ are indeterminate.
'Limit $=\infty$' describes behaviour; one-sided infinite limits can disagree in sign.

board_events.latex: \text{divide every term by the highest power of } x \text{ in the denominator}

board_events.text: Procedure C — at a jump, never substitute; split into LHL and RHL.

board_events.latex: \text{just below } n:\ [x] = n-1; \quad \text{just above } n:\ [x] = n

board_events.text: Equal and finite $\Rightarrow$ limit exists; otherwise it does not.

segments.text: Before the mechanics, four assumptions that keep you honest when infinity is involved.

First and most important: infinity is a direction, not a number. You cannot do ordinary arithmetic with it. Infinity minus infinity, and infinity over infinity, are indeterminate — they must be resolved, never assumed to be zero or one.

Second, 'limit equals infinity' describes behaviour, not a value — it records how the limit fails. And third, one-sided infinite limits can disagree in sign: one over x runs to plus infinity from the right of zero, but minus infinity from the left.

Now Procedure A, for a rational limit as x goes to infinity. Divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of x in the denominator, then send each one over x to the k to zero. The survivors give the answer.

Procedure B, the infinity minus infinity surd trick. A difference of two roots is indeterminate, so rationalise by the conjugate to turn it into a single fraction, then divide by the highest power. Root x squared plus b x, minus x, tends to b over two.

Procedure C, existence at a jump — for a piecewise, greatest-integer, or modulus function, never substitute. Identify which rule applies just to the left and compute the left-hand limit; do the same on the right; then compare.

For the greatest integer function near an integer n, just below n the value is n minus one; just above, it is n. The two differ by one, so the limit always fails at integers — that is the signature result.

And the comparison rule is always the same one from the very first subtopic: if the two one-sided limits are equal and finite, the limit exists and equals that common value; otherwise it does not exist.
Mechanics se pehle, chaar assumptions jo aapko imaandaar rakhti hain jab infinity involved ho.

Pehla aur sabse zaroori: infinity ek direction hai, number nahin. Aap iske saath ordinary arithmetic nahin kar sakte. Infinity minus infinity, aur infinity over infinity, indeterminate hain — inhein resolve karna hi padta hai, kabhi zero ya one maan nahin sakte.

Doosra, 'limit barabar infinity' behaviour batata hai, koi value nahin — ye record karta hai ki limit kaise fail hoti hai. Aur teesra, one-sided infinite limits sign mein disagree kar sakti hain: one over x, zero ke daayin se plus infinity tak jaata hai, par baayin se minus infinity.

Ab Procedure A, ek rational limit ke liye jaise x infinity ki taraf jaaye. Numerator aur denominator ke har term ko denominator ki highest power of x se divide kijiye, phir har one over x to the k ko zero bhej dijiye. Jo bache wo answer dete hain.

Procedure B, infinity minus infinity ka surd trick. Do roots ka difference indeterminate hai, to conjugate se rationalise karke ise ek single fraction banaiye, phir highest power se divide kijiye. Root x squared plus b x, minus x, jaata hai b over two ki taraf.

Procedure C, jump par existence — kisi piecewise, greatest-integer, ya modulus function ke liye, kabhi substitute mat kijiye. Pehchaniye kaunsa rule theek baayin par lagta hai aur left-hand limit nikaliye; wahi daayin par kijiye; phir compare kijiye.

Greatest integer function ke liye kisi integer n ke paas, n se thoda neeche value hai n minus one; thoda upar, ye hai n. Dono mein one ka farak, to integers par limit hamesha fail hoti hai — yahi signature result hai.

Aur comparison rule hamesha wahi hai bilkul pehle subtopic wala: agar dono one-sided limits barabar aur finite hain, to limit exist karti hai aur us common value ke barabar hai; warna exist nahin karti.

board_events.text: Infinity and special-case facts
For $x\to\infty$ rationals, divide by the highest power; for surds, rationalise.

segments.text: Here is the payload for this subtopic — the end-behaviour rules and the jump-function facts, all in one place.
The powers at infinity — one over x to the k tends to zero, and x to the k tends to infinity, for any positive k.

The degree rule for rational functions at infinity — compare the top degree m with the bottom degree n. If the top is smaller, the limit is zero; if they are equal, it is the ratio of leading coefficients; if the top is bigger, plus or minus infinity.
The infinite, vertical-asymptote limits — one over x squared goes to plus infinity from both sides, but one over x goes to plus infinity from the right of zero and minus infinity from the left.

The greatest integer facts at an integer n — the left limit is n minus one, the right limit is n, so the two-sided limit does not exist. But at a non-integer, box x is locally constant, so the limit simply equals box a.
For modulus and signum — the absolute value of x tends to the absolute value of a everywhere, but mod x over x does not exist at zero, with a left limit of minus one and a right limit of plus one.
And the indeterminate infinity-forms to watch for — infinity over infinity, infinity minus infinity, zero times infinity, and even zero over zero reappears here. Each one demands resolution.
The two reflexes stamped over it all — for a rational function as x goes to infinity, divide by the highest power; and for an infinity minus infinity surd, rationalise on sight.
Ye rahi is subtopic ki payload — end-behaviour rules aur jump-function facts, sab ek jagah.
Powers at infinity — one over x to the k jaata hai zero, aur x to the k jaata hai infinity, kisi bhi positive k ke liye.

Rational functions ke liye degree rule at infinity — top degree m ko bottom degree n se compare kijiye. Top chhota ho to limit zero; barabar ho to leading coefficients ka ratio; top bada ho to plus ya minus infinity.
Infinite, vertical-asymptote limits — one over x squared dono taraf se plus infinity jaata hai, par one over x, zero ke daayin se plus infinity aur baayin se minus infinity.

Greatest integer facts kisi integer n par — left limit hai n minus one, right limit hai n, to two-sided limit exist nahin karti. Par kisi non-integer par, box x locally constant hai, to limit bas box a ke barabar hoti hai.

Modulus aur signum ke liye — absolute value of x har jagah absolute value of a ki taraf jaata hai, par mod x over x, zero par exist nahin karta, left limit minus one aur right limit plus one ke saath.

Aur dhyaan rakhne layak indeterminate infinity-forms — infinity over infinity, infinity minus infinity, zero times infinity, aur zero over zero bhi yahaan phir se aata hai. Har ek resolution maangta hai.
Do reflexes jo in sabpar chhape hain — rational function ke liye jaise x infinity jaaye, highest power se divide kijiye; aur infinity minus infinity surd ke liye, dekhte hi rationalise kijiye.

board_events.text: Worked example: a rational limit at infinity
Speed trap: infinity minus infinity is not zero
The $\frac{b}{2}$ pattern: $\sqrt{x^{2}+bx}-x \to \frac{b}{2}$.
For $\infty-\infty$ surds, rationalise first — then divide by the highest power.

segments.text: Evaluate the limit as x goes to infinity of three x squared plus two x minus one, over five x squared minus x plus four.

Divide every term by x squared, the highest power in the denominator. The numerator becomes three plus two over x minus one over x squared; the denominator, five minus one over x plus four over x squared.
As x goes to infinity, every one over x to the k vanishes, leaving three over five. Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients — the degree-rule shortcut agrees.
<curious>Now the classic trap.</curious> Evaluate the limit as x goes to infinity of root x squared plus x, minus x. Writing 'infinity minus infinity equals zero' is wrong — it is indeterminate.
Rationalise by the conjugate. The numerator becomes x squared plus x, minus x squared, which is just x, over root x squared plus x, plus x.
Divide top and bottom by x, noting root x squared is x for large positive x. That leaves one over root of one plus one over x, plus one — which tends to one over two.
Notice the general pattern this fits: root x squared plus b x, minus x, always tends to b over two. Here b is one, so the answer is one-half.
So the reflex for any infinity minus infinity surd: rationalise first to make a single fraction, then divide by the highest power. Never write the difference as zero.
Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x infinity jaaye, of three x squared plus two x minus one, bata five x squared minus x plus four.
Har term ko x squared se divide kijiye, denominator ki highest power. Numerator banta hai three plus two over x minus one over x squared; denominator, five minus one over x plus four over x squared.
Jaise x infinity jaaye, har one over x to the k gaayab ho jaata hai, bachta hai three over five. Equal degrees leading coefficients ka ratio dete hain — degree-rule shortcut agree karta hai.
<curious>Ab classic trap.</curious> Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x infinity jaaye, of root x squared plus x, minus x. 'Infinity minus infinity barabar zero' likhna galat hai — ye indeterminate hai.
Conjugate se rationalise kijiye. Numerator banta hai x squared plus x, minus x squared, yaani sirf x, bata root x squared plus x, plus x.

Top aur bottom ko x se divide kijiye, ye note karte hue ki root x squared, x hai bade positive x ke liye. Bachta hai one over root of one plus one over x, plus one — jo jaata hai one over two ki taraf.
Is fit hone wale general pattern ko dekhiye: root x squared plus b x, minus x, hamesha jaata hai b over two ki taraf. Yahaan b hai one, to answer hai one-half.
To kisi bhi infinity minus infinity surd ka reflex: pehle rationalise karke ek single fraction banaiye, phir highest power se divide kijiye. Difference ko kabhi zero mat likhiye.

sections.subtopic: Limits at Infinity & Special Cases of Existence
sections.title: A disguised ∞−∞, and a greatest-integer sandwich

board_events.text: Worked example: a disguised infinity minus infinity
Advanced: a greatest-integer sandwich

segments.text: Evaluate the limit as x goes to infinity of x squared plus one, over x plus one, minus x. It looks like a rational minus x, but it hides an infinity minus infinity.
Combine over a common denominator first. The numerator becomes x squared plus one, minus x times x plus one, all over x plus one.
Expand and cancel the x squared terms: the numerator collapses to one minus x, over x plus one. The scary difference has become an ordinary rational limit.
Now equal degrees, with leading coefficients minus one on top and one on the bottom, give minus one. That is the limit.
Now a hopeless-looking one. Evaluate the limit as x goes to zero from the right, of x times box of one over x, where box is the greatest integer function.

The greatest integer resists substitution, so bound it. By definition, box of one over x equals one over x, minus the fractional part of one over x, and that fractional part lies between zero and one.
Multiply by x, which is positive. x times box one over x becomes one, minus x times the fractional part. And that second piece is trapped between zero and x.

As x goes to zero from the right, the sandwich forces x times the fractional part to zero. So the whole limit is one minus zero, which is one. <whisper>A hopeless greatest-integer expression became a clean sandwich.</whisper>
Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x infinity jaaye, of x squared plus one, bata x plus one, minus x. Ye ek rational minus x jaisa dikhta hai, par ismein ek infinity minus infinity chhupa hai.
Pehle common denominator par combine kijiye. Numerator banta hai x squared plus one, minus x into x plus one, bata x plus one.
Expand karke x squared terms cancel kijiye: numerator simat kar banta hai one minus x, bata x plus one. Wo daraawna difference ek ordinary rational limit ban gaya.
Ab equal degrees, top par leading coefficient minus one aur bottom par one, dete hain minus one. Yahi limit hai.
Ab ek hopeless-dikhne waali. Evaluate kijiye limit, jaise x zero ke daayin se jaaye, of x into box of one over x, jahaan box greatest integer function hai.

Greatest integer substitution ka virodh karta hai, to ise bound kijiye. Definition se, box of one over x barabar one over x, minus one over x ka fractional part, aur wo fractional part zero aur one ke beech hai.
X se multiply kijiye, jo positive hai. X into box one over x banta hai one, minus x into fractional part. Aur wo doosra piece zero aur x ke beech phansa hai.

Jaise x zero ke daayin se jaaye, sandwich x into fractional part ko zero par majboor kar deta hai. To poori limit hai one minus zero, yaani one. <whisper>Ek hopeless greatest-integer expression ek saaf sandwich ban gaya.</whisper>

sections.subtopic: Limits at Infinity & Special Cases of Existence
sections.title: Traps: ∞−∞, jump functions, wrong power, ∞ as a number

board_events.text: The four infinity-and-jump traps
Trap 1: treating $\infty-\infty = 0$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}=1$.
Trap 2: substituting into a jump function — split into LHL and RHL.
Trap 3: dividing by the wrong power in a rational limit at $\infty$.
Trap 4: treating $\infty$ as a number you can add or cancel.
Pro-tip: rational at $\infty$ → degree rule; surd $\infty-\infty$ → rationalise on sight.
For anything with $[\,\cdot\,]$, $|\cdot|$, signum, or a piecewise rule — split into two ends.

segments.text: Four traps close out this subtopic. Each one turns a manageable limit into a wrong answer.
Trap one, treating infinity minus infinity as zero, or infinity over infinity as one. Both are indeterminate — rationalise, or use the degree rule.

Trap two, substituting into a jump function. For box x, mod x over x, signum, or any piecewise function, you must split into left-hand and right-hand limits — direct substitution at the jump is meaningless.
Trap three, dividing by the wrong power. For rational limits at infinity, always divide by the highest power in the denominator — picking the wrong power scrambles the answer.
Trap four, treating infinity as a number. 'Limit equals infinity' is a behaviour statement, not a value you can add to or cancel like an ordinary number.
<whisper>The pro reflexes.</whisper> For any rational function at infinity, skip the algebra and use the three-case degree rule. For an infinity minus infinity surd, rationalise on sight.
And for anything with a greatest-integer bracket, a modulus, a signum, or a piecewise definition, your very first reflex is always the same: split it into left-hand and right-hand limits.
Chaar traps is subtopic ko band karte hain. Har ek ek manageable limit ko galat answer bana deta hai.
Trap one, infinity minus infinity ko zero maanna, ya infinity over infinity ko one. Dono indeterminate hain — rationalise kijiye, ya degree rule istemaal kijiye.

Trap two, jump function mein substitute karna. Box x, mod x over x, signum, ya kisi piecewise function ke liye, aapko left-hand aur right-hand limits mein baantna hi hoga — jump par direct substitution bekaar hai.
Trap three, galat power se divide karna. Infinity par rational limits ke liye, hamesha denominator ki highest power se divide kijiye — galat power chunne se answer gadbada jaata hai.
Trap four, infinity ko number maanna. 'Limit barabar infinity' ek behaviour statement hai, koi value nahin jise aap ordinary number ki tarah jod ya cancel kar sakein.

<whisper>Pro reflexes.</whisper> Kisi bhi rational function ke liye infinity par, algebra chhodkar three-case degree rule istemaal kijiye. Infinity minus infinity surd ke liye, dekhte hi rationalise kijiye.
Aur greatest-integer bracket, modulus, signum, ya piecewise definition wali kisi bhi cheez ke liye, aapka sabse pehla reflex hamesha wahi hai: use left-hand aur right-hand limits mein baant dijiye.

segments.text: Here is your complete Chapter twelve toolkit in one place. This is not new teaching — just every formula, ready for exam-day recall.
The existence test — the limit equals L exactly when the left-hand and right-hand limits both equal L and are finite.
The star algebraic limit — x to the n minus a to the n, over x minus a, is n times a to the n minus one, for all rational n.
The trigonometric junctions — sine x over x and tangent x over x both tend to one, and one minus cosine x over x squared tends to one-half.
The exponential and logarithmic junctions — e to the x minus one over x tends to one, a to the x minus one over x tends to log a, and log of one plus x over x tends to one.
The number e and the one-to-the-infinity rule — one plus x to the one over x tends to e, and a one-to-the-infinity form equals e to the limit of g times f minus one.
At infinity — one over x to the k tends to zero, and the rational degree rule: smaller top gives zero, equal degrees give the leading-coefficient ratio, bigger top gives plus or minus infinity.
The derivative definition — the slope of the tangent and the instantaneous rate — and it exists exactly when the left-hand and right-hand derivatives agree. Differentiable implies continuous.

The standard derivatives — x to the n gives n x to the n minus one; e to the x is its own derivative; a to the x gives a to the x log a; log x gives one over x; sine gives cosine; and cosine gives minus sine.
And the rules that combine them all — the product rule with its cross term, the quotient rule, and the chain rule. That is the whole chapter in one toolkit.
Ye rahi aapki poori Chapter twelve toolkit ek jagah. Ye koi naya teaching nahin — bas har formula, exam-day recall ke liye taiyaar.
Existence test — limit barabar L tabhi jab left-hand aur right-hand limits dono barabar L hon aur finite hon.
Star algebraic limit — x to the n minus a to the n, bata x minus a, hai n into a to the n minus one, har rational n ke liye.
Trigonometric junctions — sine x over x aur tangent x over x dono jaate hain one, aur one minus cosine x over x squared jaata hai one-half.
Exponential aur logarithmic junctions — e to the x minus one over x jaata hai one, a to the x minus one over x jaata hai log a, aur log of one plus x over x jaata hai one.
Number e aur one-to-the-infinity rule — one plus x to the one over x jaata hai e, aur ek one-to-the-infinity form barabar e to the limit of g into f minus one.
Infinity par — one over x to the k jaata hai zero, aur rational degree rule: chhota top deta hai zero, equal degrees dete hain leading-coefficient ratio, bada top deta hai plus ya minus infinity.
Derivative definition — tangent ka slope aur instantaneous rate — aur ye tabhi exist karti hai jab left-hand aur right-hand derivatives agree karein. Differentiable, continuous ko imply karta hai.

Standard derivatives — x to the n deta hai n x to the n minus one; e to the x apna derivative; a to the x deta hai a to the x log a; log x deta hai one over x; sine deta hai cosine; aur cosine deta hai minus sine.
Aur wo rules jo in sabko combine karte hain — product rule apne cross term ke saath, quotient rule, aur chain rule. Yahi poora chapter ek toolkit mein.

sections.title: Chapter 12 cheat sheet: exam-day recall

board_events.text: Chapter 12 cheat sheet: exam-day recall
Decision guide, step 1: substitute. A finite number is the answer.
Step 2: got $\frac{0}{0}$? Factor and cancel, rationalise a surd, or route through a junction.
Step 3–5: $x\to\infty$ → degree rule; $1^{\infty}$ → $e^{\lim g(f-1)}$; jump → LHL vs RHL.
Limit $\neq$ function value; $\frac{0}{0}$ means resolve, not 'does not exist'.
Radians only for $\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$; match the argument; square the $k$ for $1-\cos$.
$\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}\to 1$ but $\frac{a^{x}-1}{x}\to\ln a$ — only base $e$ is clean.
Product rule has a cross term; chain rule keeps the inside derivative.
$\infty-\infty \neq 0$; jumps need LHL vs RHL; differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous, not conversely.

segments.text: Finally, the exam-day cheat sheet — the decision guide and the top traps, distilled for the last look before the paper.
Decision guide, step one — always substitute first. If you get a finite number, that is the limit, and you are done.
Step two — got zero over zero? Resolve it: factor and cancel for a rational, multiply by the conjugate for a surd, or reshape a trig, exponential, or log form into a standard junction.

Steps three to five — if x goes to infinity, use the degree rule or rationalise a surd; if it is a one-to-the-infinity form, lift to e to the limit of g times f minus one; and if it is a jump function, split into left and right limits.
The two conceptual anchors — the limit is not the function value, f of a is irrelevant; and zero over zero means resolve, never 'zero' and never 'does not exist'.
The standard-limit anchors — sine x over x equals one only in radians; match the argument, so sine k x over x is k; and square the k in one minus cosine k x over x squared.
And the base anchor — e to the x minus one over x tends to one, but a to the x minus one over x tends to log a. Only base e gives a clean one.

The derivative anchors — the product rule always has its cross term, u dash v plus u v dash; and the chain rule always keeps the inside derivative, so derivative of sine of x squared is two x cosine of x squared.

<whisper>The last three reflexes before the paper.</whisper> Infinity minus infinity is never zero, rationalise it; jump functions always need left versus right; and differentiable implies continuous, but never the reverse.
Aakhir mein, exam-day cheat sheet — decision guide aur top traps, paper se pehle aakhri nazar ke liye nichod kar.
Decision guide, step one — hamesha pehle substitute kijiye. Finite number mila to wahi limit hai, aur aap done.
Step two — zero over zero mila? Resolve kijiye: rational ke liye factor karke cancel, surd ke liye conjugate se multiply, ya trig, exponential, ya log form ko standard junction mein reshape kijiye.

Steps three se five — agar x infinity jaaye, degree rule ya surd rationalise; agar one-to-the-infinity form ho, e to the limit of g into f minus one par uthaiye; aur agar jump function ho, left aur right limits mein baantiye.
Do conceptual anchors — limit function value nahin hai, f of a irrelevant hai; aur zero over zero ka matlab resolve, kabhi 'zero' nahin aur kabhi 'does not exist' nahin.
Standard-limit anchors — sine x over x barabar one sirf radians mein; argument match kijiye, to sine k x over x hai k; aur one minus cosine k x over x squared mein k ko square kijiye.
Aur base anchor — e to the x minus one over x jaata hai one, par a to the x minus one over x jaata hai log a. Sirf base e ek clean one deta hai.

Derivative anchors — product rule mein hamesha cross term hota hai, u dash v plus u v dash; aur chain rule hamesha inside derivative rakhta hai, to derivative of sine of x squared hai two x cosine of x squared.

<whisper>Paper se pehle aakhri teen reflexes.</whisper> Infinity minus infinity kabhi zero nahin, ise rationalise kijiye; jump functions ko hamesha left versus right chahiye; aur differentiable, continuous ko imply karta hai, par ulta kabhi nahin.
